summary:
Tyumen Oblast stands under the Russian national framework, which operates identically across all of the country's regions. The UK Home Office country policy and information note on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression (June 2025, assessment section updated 11 June 2025) records no region-specific findings; it sets the national conditions in force here and everywhere else in Russia.

Russia presents severe legal and physical risks for transgender visitors, and the position has deteriorated sharply since 2022. Legal gender recognition and gender-affirming care were banned outright in 2023, when the law prohibiting gender reassignment surgery and legal gender changes on official documents was signed; the Supreme Court designated the "international LGBT movement" an extremist organisation in November 2023; and the expanded propaganda law criminalises public expression, including anything said to justify gender transition.

Same-sex activity is not criminalised, but same-sex marriage and gender transition are banned, trans-specific healthcare was effectively banned in 2023, and no discrimination legislation based on sexual orientation or gender identity covers housing, healthcare or employment.

'Gay propaganda' offences carry fines up to 400,000 roubles (about £3,600) for individuals or up to 15 days' detention, and repeat offences can bring criminal prosecution with up to four years in prison. Participation in the designated extremist movement is punishable by two to six years' imprisonment and organising by six to ten years.

Foreigners who violate these laws face arrest, up to 15 days' detention and deportation, and official national government warnings explicitly tell LGBT travellers of this. The US State Department travel advisory for Russia is Level 4, Do Not Travel, and carries warnings directed at LGBT travellers.

Between December 2022 and March 2024 at least 139 people were affected by enforcement of anti-LGBT+ laws. The Home Office assesses that trans people, publicly active LGBT+ advocates and those in the North Caucasus are likely to face treatment amounting to persecution, and affirms that LGBT+ people in Russia, including the autonomous republic of Chechnya, constitute a particular social group under the refugee convention, which sets the assessment standard for UK asylum claims.
tangentialFactors:
Human Rights Watch reported on 30 June 2025 that Russian courts issued 101 extremism-related convictions, approximately 98 administrative and three criminal, tied to the designation of the "International Public LGBT Movement". The Supreme Court ruling of November 2023 entered into force in January 2024 and opened the way to arbitrary prosecutions of LGBT people and their supporters; the same organisation called on governments to offer safe haven to those fleeing Russia.

Between January 2024 and June 2025 at least 20 people faced criminal charges under the designation, two of them sentenced to prison and one found dead by suicide in pretrial detention. The Associated Press reported in December 2024 that a Russian man detained on extremism-related charges over an LGBTQ+ travel agency was found dead in a pretrial detention facility.

Separately, 81 people across 98 court cases were found guilty of administrative offences for displaying banned symbols, with fines up to 2,000 roubles and repeat displays punishable under the criminal code by up to four years in prison. On 15 May 2025 investigators charged three publishing-house staff under article 282.2 for selling fiction exploring LGBT themes, an offence carrying up to 12 years.

Enforcement volume has grown with its severity. Meduza reported on 19 June 2025 that cases under Russia's propaganda laws have grown eighteenfold over the past decade, and that fines under those statutes brought more than 60 million rubles ($765,300) into the state budget in the two years preceding.

The speed of the post-designation crackdown was documented by The Guardian on 17 January 2024: within 48 hours of the Supreme Court's ruling, masked police raided LGBTQ-friendly Moscow bars, where about 100 patrons at one venue were ordered to face walls, searched and photographed, while at least two other venues were raided the same night.

The Moscow Times reported on 23 June 2025 that arrests, club raids and extremism charges defined LGBTQ+ life in Russia through 2025, and carried a St Petersburg queer woman's description of herself as "a second-class citizen" after the extremist designation.
localsOnly:
Residents of Tyumen Oblast live under the same prohibitions as visitors, but with the added exposure of permanent address, employment and medical records. No discrimination legislation based on sexual orientation or gender identity covers housing, healthcare or employment, so refusals of service or dismissal have no statutory remedy, and legal gender transition cannot be obtained on any Russian document.

Administrative exposure is routine rather than exceptional: displaying a banned symbol draws a fine up to 2,000 roubles on first instance, and a repeat display moves the same conduct into the criminal code at up to four years. Advocacy and publishing carry heavier exposure, as shown by the article 282.2 charges against three publishing-house staff on 15 May 2025.

Coercion directed at trans people is documented. BBC Russian reported on 27 July 2024 on "Ada", a transgender woman lured by relatives in summer 2021 to a conversion-therapy centre near Novosibirsk in Siberia, where she was held for nine months and forced to take testosterone, pray and perform manual labour before escaping when police responded to a phone she had found.

For residents considering flight, the UK Home Office note treats LGBT+ people in Russia, including the autonomous republic of Chechnya, as a particular social group under the refugee convention, and assesses trans people and publicly active LGBT+ advocates as likely to face persecution, which governs the standard applied to UK asylum claims.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source in this inventory records enforcement activity, raids, prosecutions or court decisions in Tyumen Oblast itself. Every figure above is national, and whether oblast-level prosecutors or courts have brought extremism or propaganda cases here is unresolved and not sourced.

Entry and border-screening rules for transgender travellers entering Russia on documents that do not match presentation are not covered by any of these sources. Whether Tyumen's checkpoints or airports apply any trans-specific document check is not sourced.

Nothing in the inventory establishes the local availability or refusal of medical care, identity documents, legal representation or support services within Tyumen Oblast. The status of any LGBT venues, community organisations or safe houses in Tyumen city is not sourced.

The US State Department Level 4 advisory and the UK Home Office note are foreign-government assessments rather than Russian law; their dates and revisions are reported as published, and no source here establishes how either is applied at Russian points of entry.
